clue.text: Pale French fellow, say, back in shape

parts.note: the French word for white or pale is blanc
a fellow is a man

indicators.note: back tells us the abbreviation for 'say' is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated EG

explanation.surface: A pallid Frenchman, for example, has returned to fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns EG into GE. 'Shape' is an old word for a moulded pudding, so 'in shape' is not fitness at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A shape was the traditional name for a dessert set in a mould, such as a milk jelly turned out onto a plate.

clue.text: Body of cart made fast by mercenary Americans?

definitions.meaning: the main body of a cart or wagon carries this name
money-grubbing Americans make a quick dollar, in the idiom a fast one

explanation.walkthrough: 'made fast' means earned quickly, not tied down.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the frame of a wagon and American slang for a dollar.

clue.text: Publicizes stylish form of transport

parts.note: to air a matter is to publicize it
hip means fashionable

explanation.surface: Someone advertises a smart way to travel.
explanation.definitionFit: A powered lighter-than-air craft, a means of travel.

clue.text: This tribunal, it's ' said, dismissed a Latin poet

indicators.note: it's said means the phrase is spoken, so it is the sound that is entered
this word says the answer is heard rather than seen: it sounds like the word it governs

parts.note: in cricket a batsman is dismissed when caught, and Martial was a Roman epigrammatist

explanation.surface: A court has thrown out the case of a classical author.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech 'caught' rhymes with 'court'; caught is a cricket dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: A military court that tries members of the armed forces.

clue.text: Supporters' job, dividing drinks

indicators.note: dividing means the job splits the drinks in two

parts.note: ales are drinks
a post is a job

explanation.surface: A fan's role is handing out drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Christ's twelve disciples, and by extension ardent advocates of any cause.

clue.text: Carefree spirit of Macheath's creator

parts.note: Macheath is the highwayman of The Beggar's Opera by John Gay, so the quality of that writer, spelt as a noun from his surname, is high spirits

explanation.walkthrough: John Gay wrote The Beggar's Opera, whose hero is Macheath; his 'spirit' is merriment.
explanation.definitionFit: Merriment and light-heartedness, a state of cheerful high spirits.

clue.text: O'Neill's leading character in novel footwear

indicators.note: in tells us the first letter goes inside the novel's title

parts.note: She is Rider Haggard's novel

indicators.note: the leading character of a word is its first letter, here of the playwright's name

explanation.surface: A playwright's hero appears in fiction about fancy footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: O'Neill's 'leading character' sounds like a role in one of his plays, but it is just his initial O, placed inside SHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Footwear is anything worn on the feet, and this is the commonest example.

clue.text: Mansion accommodating ' geriatric case

indicators.note: accommodating means the mansion holds the other word inside it

parts.note: a hall is a large country house
geriatric means old

explanation.surface: A stately home houses an elderly patient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' suggests a medical case among the geriatrics; it is luggage.
explanation.definitionFit: A large travelling bag that takes everything, a type of luggage.

clue.text: Key seat tried out in the spring

parts.note: E is a musical key

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of seat and tried are put out of order

explanation.surface: A crucial seat was tested in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' looks like an adjective, important; it is the musical key E.
explanation.definitionFit: The festival season around Easter, falling in springtime.

clue.text: Plenty of almost pure cocoa in — the recipe

indicators.note: a recipe is a set of instructions for mixing things, so the letters are mixed into a new order
almost means the word pure loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A recipe calls for nearly pure cocoa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims PURE to PUR; PUR, COCOA and IN are then rearranged as the 'recipe' says.
explanation.definitionFit: The horn of plenty is a symbol of abundance, and the word now means an abundant supply.

clue.text: A reduced state, sad to say

indicators.note: reduced means the name of the state is cut short, losing its last two letters

parts.note: Alaska is a US state

explanation.surface: A country fallen on hard times is regrettable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' cuts ALASKA to its first four letters; the 'A' that opens the clue is part of the surface reading.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of regret, used where one might say 'unfortunately'.

clue.text: Very bad month! Raced around madly, being reckless!

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters surround the other pieces
madly signals that the letters of raced are rearranged

parts.note: very bad can mean evil
May is a month

explanation.surface: A terrible month spent rushing about in a frenzy.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation marks make it read as a grumble about a bad month; the anagram splits so that one letter sits in front and four behind the inserted words.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerfully careless of danger or consequences; a synonym of rash.

clue.text: Young woman taking wine after church

indicators.note: after means the wine comes after the church in the answer

parts.note: IT is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it

explanation.surface: A girl has a glass of wine after the service.
explanation.definitionFit: An old, slightly dismissive word for a pert girl or slip of a lass.

clue.text: Championship attendant starting a book

parts.note: a championship is a title won in sport
a page is a boy attendant

explanation.surface: A tournament winner's helper is getting a book under way.
explanation.definitionFit: The leaf at the front of a volume giving its name and author.

clue.text: Its tinkling said to be the death: of the telephone man

indicators.note: said to be tells us the phrase is heard spoken, so its sound gives the answer

parts.words: the death: of the telephone man
parts.note: to slay is to put to death, and Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone

explanation.surface: A ringing phone is said to be fatal to its inventor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its tinkling' points to the answer as the thing that tinkles; the rest sounds like 'slay Bell'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small jingling bell hung on a horse's harness, known for its tinkle.

clue.text: Badly-led opera, with declining listeners?

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of the next two words are put in a wrong order

explanation.surface: A poorly conducted opera loses its audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'listeners' are ears, not an audience; 'declining' means drooping, not falling in number.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes an animal, such as a rabbit, whose ears hang down rather than stand up.

clue.text: Charge it for audience to the band

indicators.note: for audience means the words are heard spoken, so their sound is what counts

parts.note: to charge something is to fill it, as one charges a glass

explanation.surface: A bill is presented to the musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' looks like the musicians but is a strip of ribbon worn round the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow headband or ribbon for binding the hair.

clue.text: You and I avoided being seen, outside the plant

indicators.note: outside means the first word goes around the second

parts.note: to duck is to bob down out of sight
you and I together are we

explanation.surface: We hid out of view behind the factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a factory; it is a water plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny floating water plant that covers ponds.

clue.text: Girl entering during meal without a welcome

indicators.note: entering means the girl's name goes inside the other letters

parts.note: during can be expressed as in

indicators.note: without means the letter A is removed from the meal

parts.note: tea is a light meal
Vi is a girl's name, short for Violet

explanation.surface: A girl turns up at dinner and nobody greets her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a welcome' reads as one phrase, but 'without a' trims TEA to TE, and VI enters IN + TE.
explanation.definitionFit: To ask someone to come is to bid them welcome, both as verbs.

clue.text: State in East keeping small quantity of cows.

indicators.note: keeping means the outer letters hold the small quantity inside

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for Virginia
in gives its own letters
E is the compass abbreviation for east
cc, a cubic centimetre, is a small quantity

explanation.surface: A state in the east holds a few head of cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: As an adjective the answer means bovine, from Latin vacca, a cow.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to cattle, from the Latin for a cow.

clue.text: Dated teenager put inside due to disturbance

indicators.note: put inside means the teenager is placed within the rearranged letters
disturbance tells us the letters of due to are stirred up

parts.note: a Mod was a teenager of the 1960s British youth cult

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned youth was jailed because of a riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put inside' suggests prison; here it places MOD inside OUTED, the anagram of DUE TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no longer in fashion or use is out of date.

clue.text: Boy's contrivance for hoisting heavy weights

definitions.meaning: a crane with a pivoting jib, also a frame over an oil well

explanation.definitionFit: Both a male first name and a lifting crane, named after a 17th-century hangman.

clue.text: Cotton firm Miss Liddell nearly invested in

indicators.note: invested in means the shortened name is placed inside the firm

parts.note: CO is short for company

indicators.note: nearly means the name loses its last letter

parts.note: Alice Liddell inspired Lewis Carroll's Alice

explanation.surface: A textile company has money from a young lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Alice Liddell was the girl for whom Lewis Carroll wrote Alice in Wonderland; 'nearly' trims ALICE to ALIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain-woven fabric made of cotton.

clue.text: Finn behind the manufacture of coarse linen?

parts.note: Huck Finn is Mark Twain's hero
aback means behind, toward the rear

explanation.surface: Mark Twain's boy lags behind at the linen mill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finn' looks like a Finnish person; it is Huckleberry Finn's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A coarse, absorbent towelling fabric woven from linen or cotton, a product of the loom.

clue.text: Court in Magyar dress

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone appears in court in Hungarian costume.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclosed open space beside a building, a courtyard.

clue.text: A sailor left one reviling a drug addict

indicators.note: left means the sailor departs from the word for one reviling

parts.note: someone who reviles another hurls abuse
AB, able seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor walked out on someone who insults a junkie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like the direction; it means went away, taking AB out of ABUSER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who takes drugs habitually, a consumer of narcotics.

clue.text: Islamic ruler gives backing to literary composition

indicators.note: gives backing to means the composition is read from back to front

parts.note: a rime is a poem, as in Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner

explanation.surface: A Muslim leader sponsors a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives backing to' looks like patronage, but it reverses RIME.
explanation.definitionFit: A title for a Muslim prince or commander, such as the rulers of Gulf states.

clue.text: Motion study of cows by Cam? It's'crazy

parts.note: kine is an old plural of cow

indicators.note: crazy tells us the letters of Cam and it's are jumbled

parts.note: It's gives its own letters without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether studying cattle beside Cambridge's river is mad.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cam is Cambridge's river; 'crazy' rearranges CAM + ITS to MATICS.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of mechanics dealing with movement without regard to the forces causing it.

clue.text: The town Pistol swore by!

definitions.meaning: a market town in Staffordshire, England
in Shakespeare's Henry V Pistol swears by the Welsh emblem vegetable that Fluellen later makes him eat

explanation.walkthrough: Pistol is a character in Henry V, not a firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a Staffordshire market town and the vegetable worn as a Welsh emblem share the name.

clue.text: Flighty type providing club with spirits

parts.note: a wood is a type of golf club
pecker is British slang for courage or spirits, as in keep your pecker up

explanation.surface: A frivolous person supplies a golf club with drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spirits' suggests alcohol; it means morale, from the British phrase 'keep your pecker up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird, and so a creature of flight, that drills into tree bark.
